summary: Planning a walk on Mars means searching many archives, and one wrong step can cost a mission. Olympus Walk App puts official NASA and USGS data on one web map of Gale Crater: terrain and slope, thermal infrared (THEMIS), mineralogy, the latest available rover weather conditions (Curiosity REMS), and rover positions and routes. Routes are calculated with the A* algorithm. An AI assistant explains each result and warns inside caution zones. A Caution Zones panel, based on the Outer Space Treaty and COSPAR policy, guides responsible exploration, and a 3D astronaut simulator lets users practice. Every feature is labeled built, simulated or concept.
details:
THE CHALLENGE AND OUR ANSWER

The challenge asks for an integrated, layered view of a location or route on Mars that combines data from multiple NASA science missions and helps a human explorer plan and carry out a successful Marswalk. Olympus Walk App answers each part. Integrated, layered view: one web map with relief and elevation, thermal infrared (THEMIS), mineralogy, and rover positions and routes, built on USGS Gale terrain data and NASA Mars Trek. Current conditions: a panel with the latest available rover weather data (Curiosity REMS), shown with date and source. Plan and carry out the walk: routes are calculated with the A* algorithm, an AI assistant explains the results and warns inside caution zones, the Caution Zones panel guides responsible exploration, and a 3D astronaut simulator lets users practice. Discoveries: the mineralogy and infrared layers help choose where to look, while planetary protection rules help keep sites of scientific interest free of contamination.

WHAT IT DOES

- Multi-layer map: relief and elevation, thermal infrared (THEMIS), mineralogy, environmental conditions, and rover positions and routes, labeled as real or simulated. Icons and a legend explain every layer.

- Conditions panel: the latest available conditions with date and source. NASA publishes this data in batches, so we never present it as real time.

- Route calculation: the app processes NASA and USGS data and calculates routes with the A* algorithm. No AI is used in the calculation; the assistant only explains the result.

- AI assistant (Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite): explains in plain language the data the app has already calculated for any selected point or route, and shows a warning when that point is inside a caution zone. The language model explains; it does not decide routes or invent data.

- Caution Zones panel: four rules from the Outer Space Treaty (Article IX) and the COSPAR planetary protection policy: Protect the Martian environment, Watch for special regions, Assess the terrain before moving, Follow mission protection measures. The panel informs; it does not certify that a route is safe.

- 3D astronaut simulator, opened with a button from the web app: the player controls an astronaut who explores Mars, analyzes the terrain, collects scientific samples, avoids hazards and manages the resources of the suit to complete missions safely, respecting planetary protection principles.

CREATIVITY

- We start from what exists. Tools such as NASA Mars Trek visualize and measure Mars very well. Olympus Walk improves on that by adding, in the same interface, route calculation, an AI assistant that explains each result and a Caution Zones panel based on space law.

- One world, three uses: planning (map, routes and assistant), responsible exploration (Caution Zones) and practice (3D simulator).

- Honesty as a feature: every function is labeled built, simulated or concept, and every datum carries its date and source. The AI only explains numbers the app has already calculated, so its answers can be traced.

DIVERSITY

A team of six that divided into subgroups and assigned work by strength. Berenice Aracelly Guerrero García, a fourth-year secondary school student, directed the project and coordinated every subgroup. The slides subgroup was Perla del Milagros Ruiz Paredes (graphic design: interface, icons, legend, logo and pitch video), Aracelly, and Valeria Brissa Lavalle Escobedo (space law and international relations: Caution Zones panel, planetary protection research and support on the slides). Sebastián Andrés Núñez Espinoza (Management and Senior Leadership student) also created the astronaut simulator, reviewed whether the project was viable, and checked the English. On the engineering side, Darwin Mendel (systems engineering) built the web platform and Juan José Meza Huanacune (software engineering) processed the NASA and USGS data, built the route calculation and the public GitHub repository. The result is a working prototype with a legal and scientific foundation.

RELEVANCE

- It delivers what the challenge asks: an interactive Mars map that integrates NASA data in layers, plus guidance to move safely.

- Ease of use: it runs in the browser from a public link, in English, with no installation, clear icons, a legend and one assistant to ask.

- Utility: a planner sees terrain, infrared, mineralogy and rover conditions together, instead of searching each archive.

IMPACT

- Problem: scattered Martian data makes route planning slow and error-prone. It is a concrete problem and we solve it with a working prototype.

- Who benefits: scientists and engineers (one place to review data), astronauts and mission personnel (context and warnings, even without geological training), and students and curious people (explore Mars and practice in the simulator).

- Reach: the code is public and the method does not depend on one place. Any rover or region with published data can be added.

- We report benefits as qualitative. We did not measure time saved or safety gains, and we do not claim them.

VALIDITY

- Built on official NASA and USGS sources, each listed in the data fields.

- Routes use the A* algorithm on processed terrain data, a standard method for path planning.

- Honest limits: conditions are the latest available data, not real time; simulated and concept features are labeled as such; the language model only explains calculated data.

- Planetary protection is grounded in the Outer Space Treaty (Article IX), the COSPAR policy (2026) and the NASA Planetary Protection Handbook. The panel separates legal obligations from technical recommendations.

- It relies on the same kind of public data that rover planning teams use, such as imagery and terrain analysis described by NASA/JPL.

PRESENTATION

Our pitch tells the story in the order the challenge asks: the problem, our solution, the proof (real NASA data and a working prototype), the team, the benefits and the next step. Full documentation and public code are available.

FUTURE PROJECTION (next steps, concept)

- Astronaut position tracking and a return route.

- Short-term environmental prediction (humidity, dust), only with a model we can demonstrate.

- Points of interest such as possible water and minerals, with their status.

- Asynchronous communication through Mars relay orbiters, designed around the 4 to 24 minute light delay.

- More rovers and regions, using the same method.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Web frontend (MVC-style architecture) deployed on Vercel, integrating NASA Trek mapping and public NASA and USGS datasets. Code on GitHub.

- Route calculation: A* algorithm.

- AI assistant: Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, used only to explain calculated data in natural language.

- Design and collaboration: Adobe Illustrator for the logo; Adobe Premiere for the pitch video,flow ai

Source code (public): https://github.com/olympus-walk
